title: Clean water, hidden risks: New technology reveals neurotoxicity missed by conventional water quality monitoring
summary: A photograph of an orchestra can tell you whether the musicians are on stage and their instruments are intact. But it cannot tell you whether they are playing in harmony. Even when every musician is present, a subtle loss of coordination can change the entire performance.

DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.6c10445 A photograph of an orchestra can tell you whether the musicians are on stage and their instruments are intact. But it cannot tell you whether they are playing in harmony. Even when every musician is present, a subtle loss of coordination can change the entire performance. Neuronal networks work in much the same way. Individual neurons may retain their normal appearance, yet the electrical signals coordinating their activity can become disrupted. Looking at neuronal structure alone may therefore miss important changes in network function. This led me to wonder whether listening to neuronal networks could reveal subtle disruptions caused by complex mixtures of environmental contaminants. Listening to neuronal networks Environmental water contains complex mixtures of pharmaceuticals, pesticides, industrial chemicals and their transformation products. Identifying individual contaminants is important, but understanding how they interact and affect biological systems as a mixture is far more challenging. Various effect-based methods have been developed to complement chemical analysis. Yet assessing subtle changes in neuronal network function directly in complex whole-water samples remains challenging. Because neurons communicate through electrical signals, I wondered whether recording these signals could provide a more direct way to assess their responses to environmental exposures. My colleagues and I therefore developed an in vitro functional neurotoxicity testing method, or iFNT, based on high-density microelectrode arrays . We cultured primary rat cortical neurons on the chips, allowing electrodes to simultaneously record electrical activity across interconnected networks. By analyzing 14 electrophysiological parameters related to neuronal firing, bursting and network synchronization, we constructed multidimensional profiles of neuronal network function. Our study is published in the journal Environmental Science &; Technology . Hearing effects that other measurements may miss We first tested individual neuroactive chemicals and a representative mixture, comparing iFNT with a conventional neurite outgrowth (NOG) assay that measures structural changes. The difference was substantial. For individual compounds, iFNT showed 5- to more than 500-fold greater sensitivity than NOG. For the chemical mixture, the sensitivity was about 50-fold greater. Some compounds produced detectable functional responses at concentrations as low as 10⁻⁸ M. These findings suggest that electrophysiological profiling can reveal chemical effects that may not be detected as readily through changes in neurite morphology. They also demonstrate the value of examining neuronal network function alongside structural measurements. However, laboratory-prepared chemicals represent only part of the environmental picture. Real-world water contains mixtures of known and unidentified substances, whose combined effects cannot always be predicted by measuring individual compounds. Could iFNT capture these effects in actual environmental samples? Taking the approach into real-world water We applied iFNT to whole-water samples collected from municipal wastewater treatment plants and their receiving waters. Importantly, the samples were tested without solid-phase extraction or preconcentration. This approach allowed us to assess the biological effects of the water samples more directly. The results were consistent with our findings from reference chemicals. Compared with NOG, iFNT showed 3- to 145-fold greater sensitivity for whole-water samples, with a median improvement of approximately 25-fold. Thus, electrophysiological profiling could detect functional responses in complex environmental mixtures without preconcentration. Subscribe A different perspective on water quality Testing real-world samples raised another question: Do conventional measures of wastewater quality reflect the same biological effects captured by neuronal network activity? We compared iFNT profiles across wastewater treatment stages with routine water-quality indicators, including chemical oxygen demand, ammonia nitrogen, total nitrogen and total phosphorus. No statistically significant correspondence was found between these indicators and the electrophysiological profiles. We also found no significant correspondence between iFNT profiles and toxicity endpoints measured in zebrafish embryos .
